results.title: Holy visit
results.text: This is a Shiva Temple. From the moment we stepped in, the sacred feeling and divine enthusiasm took over us. Would be great to visit during Shivaratri :)

results.title: Deeply moving to visit
results.text: Death and mourning are out in the open at this huge Hindu temple on the outskirts of Kathmandu. The inner temple is closed to non-Hindus but the area across the river is open to anyone. You can almost always find at least one cremation underway, and you may be able to watch a family say goodbye. The corpse is brought down the ghat to the river's edge where close family members anoint it with the holy water. Afterward, the body is carried to a brightly decorated cremation platform. The eldest son (if there is one) lights the pyre and is expected to spend 13 days in mourning at Pashtupatinath. The ashes are swept into the river, which flows to the sacred Ganges. There are smaller temples all around where "sadhus" pose for photos, monkeys clean each other, and the homeless can find shelter. Not to be missed.

results.title: One of the most moving things I've ever done while travelling
results.text:
This is a very special place and I advise anyone visiting Kathmandu to make a stop here a priority. 

This is a holy place where the devout come to die, be cremated, and have their ashes washed down the holy river into the Ganges and eventually the ocean. 

It's believed that having your remains burned here virtually ensures you will be reincarnated as a human in your next life. 

I was told that something like 35 cremations happen every day. 

People come and pay their respects to the deceased and witness their bodies go through this final transition alongside curious tourists and onlookers alike. 

It's very moving to witness the final rituals and send off of the body and soul in such an open forum.

results.title: Most unique place I've ever been!
results.text:
This is truly a bizarre but fascinating place. This is the main Hindu temple in Kathmandu. 

There you can see monkeys, a temple that foreigners have limited access. 

I pondered the meaning of life and death there.

In one instance the son of his deceased father, started a fire on yhr corpses forhead. I was told that watching or taking photos was considered fine. 

I walked by another pyre on a different day and the skeleton more or less exploded.

Don't mean to be grim but it makes you think about life.

Another thing was to watch a yogi lift a 30 pound rock with his penis! I've been told the Japanese like this. It was not that awe inspiring. 

Once again, he told me I could take photos and video and so I did.

This area is truly crazy and unique, in a good way.

results.title: Interesting
results.text:
Interesting visit. People let you wander around freely, although this feels a bit awkward because dead bodies are being cremated.

Just be carfull with unofficial guides picking you up at the ticket office.

results.title: Intriguing experience of death
results.text:
This visit was completely unique to anything else we had done before.
We hired a guide, and he explained to us about the life/worship temple before experiencing the other side of life.

After walking around, he then explained to us the cremation process, and what there was to it such as sprinkling of rice, milk, etc. depending on the circumstances. There is nearly an ongoing duration of cremations taking place here, and as a tourist, you are able to view this process from a respectful distance.

There are many sabhus here that are more than happy to have photographs taken, but expect a small donation in return. There are also many monkeys that hang around the premises, and they appeared a little more aggressive than in other places, so just be aware.

We would definitely recommend a visit for such a unique experience as this.

results.title: A must do
results.text: Very impressive! Main spot in Kathmandu where died people get their last attention! Take some moments to relax and watch these tragic moments

results.title: Must visit
results.text: One of the highlights of Kathmandu. Beautiful, ancient temple in a serene location where bodies are cremated by the river nearby. For Hindus,  the Shiva idol is part of the 12 jyotirlingas, being the top half of the same idol that's in Kedarnath. The temple is well run. Non Hindus cannot enter inside.

results.title: An amazing experience
results.text:
This feels a bit wrong to call this place an attraction, it isn't an attraction. It is a very important part of the Nepali people's circle of life. I took a small group of teenagers as part of an expedition to Nepal. I went thinking we were intruding on a very personal event. 
It was an amazing experience, I could have stayed there for hours just sitting quietly and taking it all in. We watched the whole ceremony from the body being carried in wrapped, the deceased sons having their heads shaved, to a well alight fire, to children in the river looking for gold teeth or jewellery. The holy men were there, it was not touristy at all.
I would love to return again ....

results.title: Very important place for Hindu pilgrims
results.text:
The visit to the cremation site could be somewhat disturbing if you are not hindu...so you need to be aware of this. Locals and guides do not pay but tourists are expected to pay the entry fee, and please remember unless you are Hindu or local you cannot view the interior of the temple.. 
walking around the grounds and seeing the cremations is definitely worth it.

results.title: important place ti visit
results.text: First of all it is a very important place both for hindu and budist people. Unfortunately not hindus are not allowed on the main temple, but you can enjoy the view from the rivrside to people on the other side, in the temple. And you can visit small Shiva temples on the open riverbank - each is housing a lingam, a fertility symbol. And you can see how people are embarked to their last journey in fire. great place to visit

results.title: Why is watching cremations a thing?
results.text:
I find this whole scenario disturbing. You pay to get into this world heritage site, and immediately are hounded by guides, that will continue to follow and harass you despite saying "no" multiple times. The place is filthy with trash as well as monkey, dog, and cow excrement. The holy men hanging around the temple seem to only be there to charge money for photo ops. The grounds around the temple are not that interesting, and only Hindus are allowed into the temple, which is understandable. I traveled with an American born Indian Hindu and he was only allowed in after intense questioning about his family origin in India, and after entry, he discovered they were charging money for blessings inside the temple.
The fact that people come here to witness the cremation ceremonies is the most disturbing thing to me. Death rites of loved ones as an attraction that people pay to see while on vacation? Just strikes me as twisted and sad. 
Go to may of the other great sites in Kathmandu instead, like Patan Durbar square, Bodinath, the Monkey temple, etc.

results.title: An old complex but very interesting
results.text: This is an old complex requiring a good bit of walking.  You cannot access the temple but can take photos outside. Guides are available for hire.

results.title: Touching experience
results.text: I strongly recommend visiting  the place to get a unique perspective of how Hinduism treats death- and therefore life. This place is not to admire beauty, architecture or to debate if it meets the UNESCO standards as other reviewers argue. The place shows you how some people deal with death , say goodbye to beloved ones and move on with life.  I recommend taking a good local guide to get the explanation of the rituals - otherwise you might get a superficial interpretation of what you see

results.title: Unusual sights
results.text:
We entered from the south and paid the $10usd entry. We were immediately set upon by tenacious vendors. 
Several cremations were underway. We wandered a bit and departed to the north. 
We noted that visitors entering the north portal were not paying an entry fee... 

All in all we only spent a half hour here.

results.title: Very interesting splice of Hindu culture
results.text: At times confronting, always intriguing. A fabulous insight into this most religious of Hindu sights.

results.title: Watching the cremations
results.text:
A really incredible place to go watch the cremations, locals and guides do not pay but tourists do to view this, and please remember unless you are Hindu or local you cannot view the interior of the temple.. 
walking around the grounds and seeing the cremations is definitely worth it though I would have loved to see more of it.

results.title: Surreal Experience
results.text: Being able to watch families cremate their loved ones was insane. The whole experience was mesmerizing and definitely worth a visit if you're in Kathmandu. Only problem was the beggars but didn't detract from the atmosphere at all.

results.title: Learn the Culture, See Cremation ceremony
results.text:
This was probably one of the most interesting sites we visited.  As you learn about much of the Hindu culture surrounding death performances.  

I would recommend this as an important site to see in KTM as it helps you learn about the culture and you get to see the process of cremations being performed and meet some holy men who have devoted their lives to God.
